claim: Mice have 13 pairs of ribs.
source: Mice have 13 pairs of ribs.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the figure caption describing the anatomy of mice.

claim: The somite gives rise to the dermis and muscles (dermatome and myotome) and to the vertebrae and ribs (sclerotome).
source: The dermatome and myotome (dark and light green) gives rise to the dermis and muscles while the sclerotome (yellow) gives rise to the vertebrae and ribs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the figure caption describing somite compartments.

claim: Without Apaf1, the axial skeleton develops normally.
source: Without Apaf1, the axial skeleton develops normally (n = 12/12, lower arms removed).
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1E and quantified with sample size.

claim: Without Shh, embryos develop without vertebrae and the proximal portion of the ribs.
source: Without Shh, embryos develop without vertebrae and the proximal portion of the ribs. Distal ribs form but are not patterned correctly (n = 17/17).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining shown in Figure 1F with sample size provided.

claim: Shh and Apaf1 double knockout neonates develop without vertebrae, proximal and distal ribs.
source: Double knock out (DKO) of both Shh and Apaf1 results in a more severe phenotype. DKO neonates develop without vertebrae, proximal and distal ribs (n = 7/7).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1G with sample size.

claim: The sternum is still present and ossifies on schedule in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.
source: The sternum is still present and ossifies on schedule.
evidence: This observation is stated in the description of the DKO phenotype.

claim: The thoracic somites contribute to all portions of the ribs.
source: Studies using chicken-quail chimera grafts have shown that the thoracic somites contribute to all portions of the ribs (Huang et al., 1994), with a the medial somite contributing to the proximal ribs while lateral somite contributes to the distal ribs (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The medial somite contributes to the proximal ribs while lateral somite contributes to the distal ribs.
source: Studies using chicken-quail chimera grafts have shown that the thoracic somites contribute to all portions of the ribs (Huang et al., 1994), with a the medial somite contributing to the proximal ribs while lateral somite contributes to the distal ribs (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Both the proximal and distal segments of the rib arise from the sclerotome compartment.
source: However, using retroviral lineage labeling which avoids the challenges of transplantation experiments, both the proximal and distal segments of the rib were shown to arise from the sclerotome compartment (Evans, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a retroviral lineage labeling study.

claim: In the absence of Shh, Pax1 expression is reduced and later lost.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of Shh, Pax1 expression is reduced and later lost; vertebrae and the proximal rib segments then fail to form while the distal cartilaginous portions of the ribs are still present, although abnormal (Fan and Tessier-Lavigne, 1994; Chiang et al., 1996; Marcelle et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Shh, vertebrae and the proximal rib segments fail to form while the distal cartilaginous portions of the ribs are still present, although abnormal.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of Shh, Pax1 expression is reduced and later lost; vertebrae and the proximal rib segments then fail to form while the distal cartilaginous portions of the ribs are still present, although abnormal (Fan and Tessier-Lavigne, 1994; Chiang et al., 1996; Marcelle et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Shh or Shh-producing cells in the floor plate and notochord, apoptosis in the somite is greatly increased.
source: Hh signaling is also well-known to be important for promoting cell proliferation, growth, and survival (Charrier et al., 2001; Thibert et al., 2003), and in the absence of Shh or Shh-producing cells in the floor plate and notochord, the apoptosis in the somite is greatly increased (Teillet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Removing Apaf1 can block cell death and rescue phenotypes in Shh null animals in the developing heart and face.
source: In previous studies, where loss of Shh results in high cell death in the developing heart and face, removing the function of Apoptotic protease-activating factor 1 (Apaf1), a central player in the mitochondrial pathway of programmed cell death, could block cell death and rescue the phenotype (Aiyer et al., 2005; Long et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apaf1 is required for the Cytochrome c and ATP-dependent activation of Caspase9 which leads to the subsequent activation of Caspase3, followed by the initiation of nuclear breakdown and proteolysis.
source: Apaf1 is required for the Cytochrome c and ATP-dependent activation of Caspase9 which leads to the subsequent activation of Caspase3, followed by the initiation of nuclear breakdown and proteolysis (Zou et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Embryos carrying null alleles for Apaf1 have vastly decreased cell death in the nervous system and exhibit disruptions of the head and face skeleton likely due to a grossly overgrown CNS.
source: Embryos carrying null alleles for Apaf1 (Apaf1 KO) have vastly decreased cell death in the nervous system and exhibit disruptions of the head and face skeleton likely due to a grossly overgrown CNS.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Interdigital death in the autopod is delayed in Apaf1 KO embryos.
source: In addition, interdigital death in the autopod is delayed (Cecconi et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apaf1 KO embryos develop to term but typically die at birth.
source: Although, the embryos develop to term, they typically die at birth and have not been examined during skeletal development.
evidence: This is stated based on previous observations.

claim: Patterning of the axial and appendicular portions is largely normal in Apaf1 KO embryos and cartilage and bone development proceeds on schedule.
source: Therefore, we investigated the skeleton of Apaf1 KO embryos and found that patterning of the axial and appendicular portions is largely normal and that cartilage and bone development proceeds on schedule, indicating that Apaf1 is not required for normal skeletal development (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Apaf1 is not required for normal skeletal development.
source: Therefore, we investigated the skeleton of Apaf1 KO embryos and found that patterning of the axial and appendicular portions is largely normal and that cartilage and bone development proceeds on schedule, indicating that Apaf1 is not required for normal skeletal development (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data and is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Shh KO animals exhibit a failure to form the vertebral column and pronounced rib cage defects.
source: As previously observed, Shh KO animals exhibit a failure to form the vertebral column and pronounced rib cage defects (Figure 1F) (Fan and Tessier-Lavigne, 1994; Chiang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data in Figure 1F and citations to previous studies.

claim: Absence of the proximal ribs was consistently observed amongst all Shh KO embryos stained for bone and cartilage (E15-18).
source: Absence of the proximal ribs was consistently observed amongst all Shh KO embryos stained for bone and cartilage (E15-18).
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: The pattern of the remaining rib segments varied in Shh KO embryos.
source: In contrast, the pattern of the remaining rib segments varied (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The cartilage portions in Shh KO embryos were distally located and never mineralized suggesting that they represented the distal costal cartilages.
source: These cartilage portions were distally located and never mineralized suggesting that they represented the distal costal cartilages.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the location and mineralization status of the cartilage.

claim: The distal rib segments in Shh KO embryos were not entirely normal as they were discontinuous, reduced in number (~7–8 instead of 13), not properly articulated with the sternum, and positioned at abnormal angles.
source: These segments were not entirely normal as they were discontinuous, reduced in number (~7–8 instead of 13), not properly articulated with the sternum, and positioned at abnormal angles.
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: The clavicle and sternum were present in Shh KO embryos, although the sternum was sometimes not completely fused and had missing or disorganized segments.
source: The clavicle and sternum were present, although the sternum was sometimes not completely fused and had missing or disorganized segments; however, it did undergo ossification on schedule.
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: The sternum in Shh KO embryos underwent ossification on schedule.
source: The clavicle and sternum were present, although the sternum was sometimes not completely fused and had missing or disorganized segments; however, it did undergo ossification on schedule.
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos exhibited an even more severe skeletal phenotype than Shh KO embryos.
source: To our surprise, instead of observing a rescue of the Shh KO phenotype, Shh;Apaf1 DKO animals exhibited an even more severe skeletal phenotype.
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos displayed features of the Shh single KO (no vertebrae and proximal ribs).
source: Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos did display features of the Shh single KO (no vertebrae and proximal ribs).
evidence: This is a direct observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: In Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, the distal portion of the ribs was missing as evidenced by the lack of alcian blue staining in the body wall.
source: However, in addition to these defects, the distal portion of the ribs was now missing as evidenced by the lack of alcian blue staining in the body wall (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Rarely, a few small pieces of cartilage were present at the lateral margin in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, near the expected location of the chondro-costal joint.
source: Rarely, a few small pieces of cartilage were present at the lateral margin, near the expected location of the chondro-costal joint (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The axial skeleton of Casp3 KO animals was grossly normal.
source: As with loss of Apaf1, the axial skeleton of Casp3 KO animals was grossly normal (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Shh;Casp3 DKO embryos exhibited a complete absence of all vertebrae, vertebral ribs and sternal ribs as was observed in the Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.
source: Shh;Casp3 DKO embryos exhibited a complete absence of all vertebrae, vertebral ribs and sternal ribs as was observed in the Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos (compare Figure 1G and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 2D and comparison to Figure 1G.

claim: The observed phenotypes when Apaf1 is removed are not due to a specific non-canonical function but rather due to a general abrogation of the programmed cell death pathway.
source: These results suggest that the observed phenotypes when Apaf1 is removed are not due to a specific non-canonical function but rather due to a general abrogation of the programmed cell death pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similarity of phenotypes between Apaf1 and Casp3 knockouts.

claim: In control embryos, evidence of normal cell death can be seen beginning as early as E9.0 as distinct periodic stripes of staining in the somites, extending to E10.5 and waning by E11.5.
source: In control embryos, evidence of normal cell death can be seen beginning as early as E9.0 as distinct periodic stripes of staining in the somites, extending to E10.5 and waning by E11.5 (Figure 2E,E', I) (Sanders, 1997; Teillet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2E,E',I and citations to previous studies.

claim: The absence of Apaf1 results in a dramatic reduction in cell death throughout the embryo, and notably absence of cell death in the somites.
source: The absence of Apaf1, however, results in a dramatic reduction in cell death throughout the embryo, and notably absence of cell death in the somites (Figure 2F,F').
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2F,F'.

claim: Shh KO embryos exhibit high cell death in the somites — with high LysoTracker-positive staining in the ventral sclerotome domain.
source: In contrast, Shh KO embryos exhibit high cell death in the somites — with high LysoTracker-positive staining in the ventral sclerotome domain (Figure 2G,G' and inset, marked with brackets).
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2G,G'.

claim: The absence of Apaf1 in Shh null embryos (Shh;Apaf1 DKOs) results in a vast reduction in LysoTracker-positive cells.
source: Interestingly, the absence of Apaf1 in Shh null embryos (Shh;Apaf1 DKOs) results in a vast reduction in LysoTracker-positive cells (Figure 2H,H').
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2H,H'.

claim: Casp3 KO embryos display a dramatic reduction in cell death compared to the normal pattern.
source: Like Apaf1 KO embryos, Casp3 KO embryos display a dramatic reduction in cell death compared to the normal pattern (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: Shh;Casp3 DKO embryos exhibit a dramatic reduction in cell death compared to the Shh KO pattern.
source: Similarly, Shh;Casp3 DKO embryos (Figure 2L), also exhibit a dramatic reduction in cell death compared to the Shh KO pattern.
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The absence of either Apaf1 or Casp3 results in an inhibition of programmed cell death even in Shh null animals.
source: Thus, the absence of either Apaf1 or Casp3 results in an inhibition of programmed cell death even in Shh null animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the LysoTracker staining data.

claim: Shh is expressed in the dorsal root ganglia, ventral neural tube, developing lungs, as well as the developing ribs themselves.
source: However, Shh is also expressed in other developing tissues that could affect somite patterning and rib formation. For example, RNA in situ hybridization reveals that Shh is also expressed in the dorsal root ganglia, ventral neural tube, developing lungs, as well as the developing ribs themselves (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Administration of tamoxifen at E8.0 did not alter Ptch1 expression in E9.0 somites indicating that the activity of Shh prior to cre-mediated deletion was sufficient for Ptch1 expression.
source: Administration of tamoxifen at E8.0 did not alter Ptch1 expression, a readout of Shh signaling, in E9.0 somites indicating that the activity of Shh prior to cre-mediated deletion (likely sometime between E8.0-E10) was sufficient for Ptch1 expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the conditional knockout experiments.

claim: Embryos with tamoxifen administration at E8.0 had no skeletal defects in the thoracic cage.
source: As a result, these embryos had no skeletal defects in the thoracic cage; later injections also failed to generate skeletal defects.
evidence: This is an observation from the conditional knockout experiments.

claim: Administration of tamoxifen at E7.0 caused a discontinuity in Shh and Ptch1 expression at E8.0.
source: However, administration of tamoxifen at the same doses at E7.0 caused a discontinuity in Shh and Ptch1 expression at E8.0 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos with tamoxifen administration at E7.0 developed with a range of Shh KO hypomorphic phenotypes.
source: Subsequently, embryos developed with a range of Shh KO hypomorphic phenotypes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The most severe phenotypes in Shh hypomorphs were very similar to Shh KO animals and lacked the vertebrae and proximal ribs.
source: Importantly, the most severe phenotypes were very similar to Shh KO animals and lacked the vertebrae and proximal ribs (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 3C,F.

claim: The distal-most sternal ribs were present but mis-patterned in Shh hypomorphs, although less severely than the Shh KO animals.
source: The distal-most sternal ribs were present but mis-patterned, although less severely than the Shh KO animals.
evidence: This is an observation from skeletal staining experiments.

claim: Being additionally null for Casp3 in Shh hypomorphs resulted in failed distal rib development.
source: Furthermore, being additionally null for Casp3 resulted in failed distal rib development (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Among the hypomorphic Shh KO animals, less severely affected animals lacked vertebrae and the proximal half of the vertebral rib, while the least affected only had abnormal vertebrae and were missing just the most proximal ends of the proximal rib.
source: Among the hypomorphic Shh KO animals, less severely affected animals lacked vertebrae and the proximal half of the vertebral rib, while the least affected only had abnormal vertebrae and were missing just the most proximal ends of the proximal rib (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal staining data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Shh signaling from the notochord and floor plate is required for normal thoracic skeletal development at stages prior to rib outgrowth and potentially even earlier.
source: Thus, these experiments indicated that Shh signaling from the notochord and floor plate is required for normal thoracic skeletal development at stages prior to rib outgrowth and potentially even earlier.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the conditional knockout experiments.

claim: High levels of Hedgehog signaling are required for normal proximal development and lower levels for distal development.
source: In addition, a comparison of the milder phenotypes vs. the more severe phenotypes suggests that high levels of Hedgehog signaling are required for normal proximal development and lower levels for distal development.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the range of hypomorphic phenotypes.

claim: Compared to Shh KO embryos, Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos were smaller and consistently delayed at E9-E12, (~3 fewer somites than average for that litter).
source: We first found that compared to Shh KO embryos, Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos were smaller (compare panels 2G', H') and consistently delayed at E9-E12, (~3 fewer somites than average for that litter; n > 6 litters) suggesting the Apaf1 plays a role in embryo size in the absence of Shh.
evidence: This is a direct observation from embryo analysis.

claim: Apaf1 plays a role in embryo size in the absence of Shh.
source: We first found that compared to Shh KO embryos, Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos were smaller (compare panels 2G', H') and consistently delayed at E9-E12, (~3 fewer somites than average for that litter; n > 6 litters) suggesting the Apaf1 plays a role in embryo size in the absence of Shh.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the size difference between Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.

claim: The expression domain of sclerotome markers Pax1 and FoxC2 are reduced in both Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, but the expression profiles were similar.
source: However, while the expression domain of sclerotome markers Pax1 and FoxC2 (Furumoto et al., 1999; Peters et al., 1999; Rodrigo et al., 2003) are reduced in both Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, the expression profiles were similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: An alteration in early somite patterning does not readily explain the difference in the final skeletal phenotype between Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO animals.
source: Thus, an alteration in early somite patterning does not readily explain the difference in the final skeletal phenotype between Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similarity of sclerotome marker expression.

claim: Sox9-expressing cells are present in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, however, in an even thinner and shorter domain than Shh KO embryos.
source: Interestingly, Sox9-expressing cells are indeed present in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, however, in an even thinner and shorter domain (Figure 4D) indicating that cartilage specification occurs in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cartilage specification occurs in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.
source: Interestingly, Sox9-expressing cells are indeed present in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, however, in an even thinner and shorter domain (Figure 4D) indicating that cartilage specification occurs in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the presence of Sox9-expressing cells.

claim: Aggregations and tight condensations could be seen in normal and Shh KO embryos.
source: Aggregations and tight condensations could be seen in normal and Shh KO embryos (Figure 4E,F;H,I).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4E,F,H,I.

claim: In Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, while some aggregation could be observed, distinct condensations were not evident.
source: However, in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, while some aggregation could be observed, distinct condensations were not evident (Figure 5G,J).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5G,J (note: likely Figure 4G,J based on context).

claim: In the body wall of Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, no expression of Col2a1, Sox9, or alcian blue staining was evident.
source: However, in the body wall of Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, no expression of Col2a1, Sox9, or alcian blue staining was evident (Figure 4M,P,S,S').
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization and alcian blue staining data shown in Figure 4M,P,S,S'.

claim: In Shh KO embryos although the distal rib anlage is smaller compared to controls, differentiation proceeds normally.
source: Thus, in summary, these assays demonstrate that in Shh KO embryos although the distal rib anlage is smaller compared to controls, differentiation proceeds normally.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differentiation marker analysis.

claim: In Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, the rib anlagen are even smaller than seen in Shh KO embryos, and while some cells turn on Sox9 and some aggregates form, they do not condense normally, and fail to differentiate.
source: However in Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos, the rib anlagen are even smaller than seen in Shh KO embryos, and while some cells turn on Sox9 and some aggregates form, they do not condense normally, and fail to differentiate.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differentiation marker analysis.

claim: Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos have smaller somites than either controls or Apaf1 KO embryos.
source: Bayesian estimates indicate that Shh KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos have smaller somites than either controls or Apaf1 KO embryos. Median estimates are Apaf1 KO = 0.92, Shh KO = 0.59 and Shh;Apaf1 DKO = 0.57, probability that the ratios are less than 1 are 0.67, 0.99, and 0.99, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of somite size measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Normal and Shh KO embryos have a similar ratio of pHH3 positive to total cells in the somite.
source: Normal and Shh KO embryos have a similar ratio of pHH3 positive to total cells in the somite (shown relative to controls).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation rate measurements.

claim: Apaf1 KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos both exhibit a decrease in the ratio of pHH3 positive to total cells.
source: While Apaf1 KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos both exhibit a decrease in the ratio of pHH3 positive to total cells.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation rate measurements.

claim: Apaf1 KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos have a reduced proliferation rate than either controls or Shh KO embryos.
source: Bayesian estimates indicate that Apaf1 KO and Shh;Apaf1 DKO embryos have a reduce proliferation rate than either controls or Shh KO embryos. Median estimates are Apaf1 KO = 0.71, Shh KO = 1.1 and Shh;Apaf1 DKO = 0.32, probability that the ratios are less than 1 are 0.91, 0.33, and 1.0, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of proliferation rate measurements shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The loss of cell death might be expected to result in increased tissue growth as has been observed in the brains of Apaf1 and Casp3 embryos.
source: The formation of smaller aggregates in the Shh;Apaf1 DKO is at first confusing since the loss of cell death might be expected to result in increased tissue growth as has been observed in the brains of Apaf1 and Casp3 embryos (Cecconi et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The simulation could represent the response to a Hh concentration gradient reliably with the percent of proximal red and distal blue cells dependent on the Hh dose and gradient steepness.
source: Using an initial fixed size and our newly defined baseline parameters, we found that the simulation could represent the response to a Hh concentration gradient reliably with the percent of proximal red and distal blue cells dependent on the Hh dose and gradient steepness (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When varying the initial size, with fixed morphogen parameters, smaller initial sizes are more proximalized as a larger percentage of the cells are under the influence of high Hedgehog signaling.
source: In addition, when varying the initial size, with fixed morphogen parameters, smaller initial sizes are more proximalized as a larger percentage of the cells are under the influence of high Hedgehog signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The generation of a highly distinct border between the two elements required that cells be programmed to sense the fate of local cells within their environment (the 'community effect').
source: Interestingly, the generation of a highly distinct border between the two elements did require that cells be programmed to sense the fate of local cells within their environment (the 'community effect') as predicted by early studies on muscle differentiation (Gurdon, 1988) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and citation to a previous study.

claim: Alterations in the rate of cell death or of proliferation, while profoundly impacting overall size, did not have a large effect on the ratios of cells that contributed to a proximal vs. distal element.
source: In addition, alterations in the rate of cell death or of proliferation, while profoundly impacting overall size, did not have a large effect on the ratios of cells that contributed to a proximal vs. distal element (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The model displays robust reproduction of a wide range of observed phenomena.
source: Thus, our model displays robust reproduction of a wide range of observed phenomena (see Video 1 for simulations for the different genotypes).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation results.

claim: Patterning can happen early when cell populations are small and thus the distances required to interpret a Hh gradient are not too great.
source: We show that patterning can happen early when cell populations are small and thus the distances required to interpret a Hh gradient are not too great.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation results.

claim: Size is regulated via mechanisms that control cell number such as initial progenitor number and proliferation rate.
source: In addition, we infer how size is regulated via mechanisms that control cell number such as initial progenitor number and proliferation rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation results.

claim: The model is essentially biphasic, with early events that define the size and fate of the progenitor populations and later events that expand the already specified population.
source: Finally, we find that our model is essentially biphasic, with early events that define the size and fate of the progenitor populations and later events that expand the already specified population.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation results.

claim: The role of Hh signaling is multi-functional and likely required for many processes during rib development including: (1) sclerotome induction, (2) maintenance of cell survival, and (3) proximal-distal specification.
source: As observed in many other contexts (Briscoe and Small, 2015), the role of Hh signaling is multi-functional and likely required for many processes during rib development including: (1) sclerotome induction, (2) maintenance of cell survival, and (3) proximal-distal specification.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results and citation to previous work.

claim: Proximal-distal specification occurs when the cells have not yet migrated long distances away from the midline and the progenitor pools are quite small.
source: In the context of the rib, we favor an early specification scenario where proximal-distal specification occurs when the cells have not yet migrated long distances away from the midline and the progenitor pools are quite small.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental and simulation results.

claim: As the embryo grows, the specified compartments would expand laterally.
source: Therefore, the transport of the Hh protein can occur over a short period of time and transport over long distances is not required to explain the results (Phase 1). Then as the embryo grows, the specified compartments would expand laterally (Phase 2) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental and simulation results.

claim: The idea of early proximal-distal specification followed by expansion to establish the initial broad proximal and distal fields has been gaining traction in the field of limb development.
source: In recent years, this idea of early proximal-distal specification followed by expansion to establish the initial broad proximal and distal fields has been gaining traction in the field of limb development ([Roselló-Díez et al., 2011; Cunningham and Duester, 2015] and reviewed in Mariani [2010]) and seems easily applicable in the case of rib patterning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tamoxifen administration at E7.0 resulted in thoracic skeletal defects similar to Shh KO embryos, while administration after E8.0 or later was not sufficient to generate a thoracic phenotype.
source: Support for a role for Shh signaling at very early somite stages (prior to E9.0), comes from our experiments where tamoxifen administration at E7.0 resulted in thoracic skeletal defects similar to Shh KO embryos (Figure 3), while administration after E8.0 or later was not sufficient to generate a thoracic phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by conditional knockout experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: BMPs are important in axial skeletal growth to maintain a chondrogenic regulatory loop.
source: These results also align with previous studies suggesting that Hh signaling is only initially required at presomitic mesoderm stages and that subsequently BMPs are important in axial skeletal growth to maintain a chondrogenic regulatory loop (Zeng et al., 2002; Stafford et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within the agent-based simulations, the length scale over which Hh concentration can influence cell fate is approximately the same as the size of the progenitor pool and most cells 'decide' their fate relatively early.
source: Indeed, within our agent-based simulations, the length scale over which Hh concentration can influence cell fate is approximately the same as the size of the progenitor pool and most cells 'decide' their fate relatively early.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Cells making late decisions become distal because they experience a very low Hh signal or become proximal due to influence from surrounding proximal cells.
source: We suggest that cells making late decisions become distal because they experience a very low Hh signal or become proximal due to influence from surrounding proximal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the simulation results.

claim: In the absence of Apaf1, somite cell death is inhibited.
source: In the context of rib development, in the absence of Apaf1, somite cell death is inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data.

claim: When modeling the absence of Apaf1 in the agent-based simulation, the proliferation rate must be moderately reduced to compensate for reduced cell death in order to achieve normal skeletal size.
source: When modeling this in our agent-based simulation, the proliferation rate must be moderately reduced to compensate for reduced cell death in order to achieve normal skeletal size.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Proliferation rate is decreased when Apaf1 is lost.
